messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arthur was sixty-two when his wife, Diane, died of a sudden pulmonary embolism on a Tuesday afternoon. She had been packing clay for his next kiln load—a thing she always did without being asked—and he found her on the studio floor, her hand still curled around a damp sponge. The paramedics told him there was nothing he could have done, but the image of that sponge stayed with him for months, a small, absurd detail that made the whole event feel both grotesque and unreal. He had been a potter for forty years, and Diane had been his collaborator, his business manager, the one who kept the orders straight and the glaze recipes organized. Without her, the studio felt hollow, the kick wheel too quiet.

Two years on, Arthur still works the clay most days, but the rhythm has changed. He no longer allows himself to feel the small satisfactions that used to punctuate a throwing session—the clean weight of a centered lump, the sudden smoothness of a pulled handle. When a bowl comes out exactly as he imagined, he sets it aside without looking at it twice and starts the next piece. Positive emotions feel unsafe to him now, like a door he is afraid to open because he does not know what will come through. He has learned to push them away before they can settle.

He has also dismantled almost every trace of Diane from the house. Her gardening gloves went into the trash; her favorite mug, the one she drank tea from every morning, is now wrapped in newspaper at the back of a closet. He cannot bear to see objects that belonged to her because each one carries a small, specific memory—the way she hummed while trimming a pot, the laugh she gave when a kiln shelf cracked. He avoids the farmers’ market where they used to buy vegetables on Saturdays, and he has stopped driving past the community center where she taught her weekly watercolor class. These places are grief reminders, and he treats them like landmines.

The most pervasive change, however, is his refusal to make any plans for the future. When a local gallery asked him to commit to a solo show in six months, he declined without explanation. When his daughter suggested a family trip for the holidays, he said he would “see how he felt” and then stopped returning her calls. Even small decisions—what to have for dinner next Friday, whether to replace the worn-out kiln shelves—feel impossible. Arthur has come to believe that planning ahead is a kind of arrogance, a presumption that the future will cooperate, and he no longer trusts that.

His wife’s sister, Margaret, visited last month and found the studio cold, the shelves only half full. She told him he was disappearing into himself. Arthur heard the worry in her voice but could not summon the energy to reassure her. He spends his days throwing pots that he does not fire, letting the clay dry and crack on the wedging table because committing to a glaze would mean deciding what the piece was for. His pottery business, once thriving, has dwindled to a few regular customers who accept his vague promises of delivery “someday.”

What finally brought him to seek help was the approach of what would have been his and Diane’s thirty-fifth wedding anniversary. Margaret made an appointment with a therapist and drove him there herself. Arthur sat in the waiting room with his hands clenched in his lap, certain that talking about any of this would only make it worse. But he also knew, with a quiet dread, that he could not go on turning away from every small joy, every memory, every tomorrow. He was tired of living in the narrow space between what he could not face and what he would not plan. He hoped the therapist might give him permission to stop holding so tightly to nothing at all.
